title: Part 108 Drone Rules Explained (2026): Current BVLOS Status | Drone Authority
text:
Part 108 Drone Rules Explained (2026): Current BVLOS Status | Drone Authority

# Part 108 drone rules, explained

The FAA's proposed route to routine beyond-visual-line-of-sight operations. It is not in effect, and a Part 107 certificate alone does not unlock it.

BVLOS · NPRM

Is Part 108 in effect? No.

As of November 7, 2026, no final rule has been published. The FAA's final rule has been at the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs since July 10, 2026, listed as Pending Review, and the FAA has said it hopes to see it published by the end of the year. Until it is published and takes effect, no operator can claim Part 108 authority. The OIRA register was checked alongside the Federal Register docket.

Two clocks to watch, neither of them a date

Executive Order 12866 gave OIRA 90 days from July 10, a window that ended October 8. The order allows one extension of up to 30 days with the OMB Director's written approval, which would run to November 7, and more time at the agency head's request. The review was still open on November 7, day 120, and the public record does not say whether either extension was used. The second clock is the statute: 49 U.S.C. 44811(c) calls for a final rule 16 months after the proposed rule is published, which counts to December 7, 2026. The FAA's Fall 2025 Unified Agenda listed the deadline as January 16, 2026 instead. We have found no FAA statement on timing newer than its September 3 year-end hope. Read the OIRA watch and the TSA roundtable notice.

BEYOND Phase 2 does not change the rule today

The FAA opened applications on August 27 for up to eight additional government-led test teams. The work can build evidence for future BVLOS rules, but a BEYOND agreement is not Part 108 and does not provide blanket flight authority.

Part 108 is the FAA's proposed framework to normalize beyond-visual-line-of-sight (BVLOS) drone flight, letting drones fly past where the pilot can see them under a standing operating framework instead of relying on case-by-case relief. The NPRM addresses delivery, surveying, agriculture, civic-interest operations, aircraft acceptance, personnel, maintenance, and automated traffic-support services. But it is a proposal. Until a final rule takes effect, operators must use the existing FAA approval path for BVLOS, commonly a Part 107 waiver.

Key facts

Status (November 7, 2026)

Final rule at OIRA since July 10, 2026, Pending Review: NOT published, NOT in effect

Statutory deadline

December 7, 2026 by the statute's count (16 months after the August 7, 2025 NPRM); the Fall 2025 Unified Agenda lists January 16, 2026

FAA's stated hope

Publication by the end of 2026 (Commercial UAV Expo, September 3)

What it covers

Routine beyond-visual-line-of-sight (BVLOS) drone operations

NPRM published

August 7, 2025

Comment period

Closed Oct 6, 2025; reopened, then closed again Feb 11, 2026

Flying BVLOS today

Use the existing FAA approval path, commonly a Part 107 waiver

Proposal structure

Part 108 operations + Part 146 automated data services

## Where the rule stands

The timeline below reflects the public rulemaking record checked November 7, 2026.

1. Aug 7, 2025

FAA and TSA publish the Part 108 NPRM, 'Normalizing UAS Beyond Visual Line of Sight Operations.'
2. Oct 6, 2025

Initial public comment period closes; heavy feedback on right-of-way, ADS-B Out, electronic conspicuity, and detect-and-avoid.
3. Jan 28, 2026

FAA reopens the comment period with seven targeted questions on electronic conspicuity and right-of-way.
4. Feb 11, 2026

Reopened comment period closes; a request to extend it further is denied.
5. Jul 10, 2026

OIRA receives the FAA's final rule, RIN 2120-AL82, for Executive Order 12866 review. The record lists it as not economically significant, with a statutory legal deadline. The FAA's Fall 2025 Unified Agenda gives that deadline as January 16, 2026. The statute, 49 U.S.C. 44811(c), sets it at 16 months after the proposed rule is published, and the NPRM was published August 7, 2025, which counts to December 7, 2026. The nominal 90-day review window runs to October 8, extendable once by 30 days.
6. Aug 27, 2026

FAA opens BEYOND Phase 2 to add up to eight government-led test teams. The program can inform future rules but does not grant automatic BVLOS authority.
7. Sep 3, 2026

At the closing keynote of Commercial UAV Expo, the FAA's Emerging Technologies Division says it hopes to see the rule published by the end of the calendar year (reported by Commercial UAV News).
8. Sep 4, 2026

TSA publishes a Federal Register notice soliciting BVLOS operators for closed technical roundtables on its Part 108 security-program requirements, to be held after the FAA and TSA final rules publish. Requests to participate are due October 19.
9. Oct 8, 2026

Day 90, the end of the nominal review window. OIRA logs two EO 12866 meetings on the rule that day. It remains Pending Review.
10. Oct 19, 2026

TSA's deadline for operators to ask for a seat at its security roundtables. The roundtables meet after the final rules publish.
11. Nov 3, 2026

DOT publishes a Privacy Act notice, DOT/FAA 860, for Part 108 and Part 146 records, with comments due December 3. It describes the final rule as issued, but OIRA still lists it as Pending Review and no final rule has appeared in the Federal Register.
12. Nov 7, 2026

Day 120, still Pending Review at OIRA. That is where one 30-day extension approved by the OMB Director would end. Executive Order 12866 also allows more time at the agency head's request. No rule text is public, and operators must use the existing FAA approval path for BVLOS.

## What Part 108 would change

The proposal moves BVLOS from a case-by-case waiver to a standing, performance-based rule. The headline elements under debate:

- Routine BVLOS at low altitude without a per-flight waiver, on a performance-based standard.
- A framework for third-party services, including UAS Traffic Management (UTM).
- Detect-and-avoid expectations so drones can sense and stay clear of other aircraft.
- Electronic conspicuity and right-of-way rules: the most contested provisions, and the focus of the reopened comment period.

## This is an operating system, not a new pilot card

The 180-page NPRM is much broader than permission for one remote pilot to look away from an aircraft. It proposes a connected operator, personnel, aircraft, maintenance, and data-service framework.

Operator authority

A permitted or certificated operator would apply for FAA authority tied to the operation, rather than treating a Part 107 card as the whole approval.

People and supervision

The proposal defines roles such as operations supervisor and flight coordinator, plus knowledge, aircraft-specific training, currency, medical-condition, drug and alcohol, and duty-rest provisions.

Aircraft and maintenance

The aircraft would need the applicable airworthiness acceptance, operating documents, maintenance controls, records, and continued-safety processes described by the proposal.

The flight itself

Area of operations, preflight planning, controlled airspace, operations over people, strategic deconfliction, conformance monitoring, right of way, Remote ID, and multiple-aircraft operations all appear in the proposed rule.

Part 146 services

A companion proposed Part 146 would certify automated data service providers that support strategic deconfliction and other services used by BVLOS operators.

## What does not change today

- A Part 107 certificate does not create Part 108 authority.
- The NPRM does not let a pilot begin routine BVLOS while the rule is still proposed.
- Airspace authorization, TFRs, security restrictions, land access, and state or local launch rules remain separate checks.
- The final rule can differ from the NPRM, including the operator, aircraft, right-of-way, and electronic-conspicuity details summarized here.

Flying BVLOS today

Existing FAA approval paths remain available. For many small-UAS operators, that means a waiver of the Part 107 visual-line-of-sight rule and a safety case for the specific operation. The proposal itself is not an approval.

Rulemaking status checked November 7, 2026; verify at faa.gov/uas. Educational, not legal advice.
